title: Container deployment
purpose: Measure what a deploy costs on this machine: building an image with a cold and a warm layer cache, writing it out and reading it back, and starting a container until it answers.

implementation.note: The build context is generated by this module rather than shipped or downloaded, so every machine builds the same thing. The startup phases run a pinned BusyBox image through the same argument-vector boundary as every other container this program starts.

dependencies: A container runtime (Docker or Podman) whose daemon is reachable
About 72 MiB of free space in the daemon's storage and the scratch directory

safety.target: images and containers this module creates, all carrying this agent's label
never: any host path inside a container
safety.note: Removal is filtered by this agent's own label rather than by a name prefix, so nothing an operator named can be in range. Images are reaped before containers, because an image cannot be removed while a container made from it exists.

sandbox.build_base: scratch. Nothing is pulled and the build runs with --network none, so it cannot be. A build FROM a real base image would mostly measure a registry, which network.transfer measures directly and under a bounded ceiling.
sandbox.startup_base: busybox@sha256:3c6ae8008e2c2eedd141725c30b20d9c36b026eb796688f88205845ef17aa213, resolved from busybox:stable-musl against Docker Hub on 2026-08-14
sandbox.why_busybox: 877 KB, one static multi-call binary, no init system and no runtime to warm up. The startup measurement has to start from something, and the right something contributes as little of its own as a running container can - so what is left is the machine creating namespaces, mounting an overlay and execing a process.
sandbox.capabilities: all dropped, no-new-privileges set, no host path mounted, no device passed. The ephemeral containers additionally get --network none and no published port.
sandbox.image_fetch: explicit and untimed, before any clock starts. An implicit pull inside `docker run` put a download inside one repetition of seven and took the coefficient of variation to 147%.

preparation: The build context is generated into the scratch directory and the base image is confirmed present before anything is timed.
calibration: None. Every figure here is the duration or rate of a fixed, identical operation, so there is no work size to calibrate to a target duration.
warmup: The cached build is preceded by the uncached one, which is what warms the layer cache. That is disclosed as a limitation rather than presented as neutral: a CI cache restored from elsewhere pays a transfer this does not measure.

workloads.description: The full build with --no-cache: every layer rebuilt
workloads.represents: A CI job with a cold cache, or the first build after a base change

workloads.description: The same build with the layer cache warm
workloads.represents: What every push after the first one costs - the common case

workloads.description: The ratio of the two above
workloads.represents: Whether the layer cache is working on this host. Deliberately the lowest-weighted metric: a machine with a slow uncached build earns a large ratio for having had further to fall

workloads.description: Writing the image to a tar archive
workloads.represents: The local half of a registry push

workloads.description: Reading it back: extraction, decompression, layer commit
workloads.represents: The local half of a registry pull, and what a rollback costs

workloads.description: Create, start, exec a trivial command, exit and remove - measured in the foreground over 7 repetitions
workloads.represents: The runtime's own price per container: namespaces, cgroups, an overlay mount, an exec. What a CI step pays before it does anything

workloads.description: From asking for a container to getting an HTTP status line out of it, over 5 repetitions
workloads.represents: What an operator waits through on a rolling restart, including port publication

repetitions.note: Fixed and not profile-dependent. The builds are measured once each - a build takes seconds, so one observation is dominated by the work rather than by noise, and a second uncached build would cost another minute to learn very little. The two startup metrics take 7 and 5 repetitions and are the only ones here with a distribution behind them, because a container start takes a few hundred milliseconds and a single sample is mostly whatever the daemon happened to be doing.

validation: A build that did not succeed produces no metric rather than a duration; a failed build finishes quickly and would read as a fast machine.
The cached build must not be slower than the uncached one. If it is, the cache did not hit and the pair describes two cold builds, so the speedup ratio is withheld.
A startup metric needs a majority of its repetitions to have succeeded. Below that the machine is failing to start containers, which is a finding rather than a set of slow samples to average.
Any metric whose coefficient of variation exceeds the stability bound raises a warning and degrades the result.
abort_conditions: no container runtime, or a runtime whose daemon does not answer
the base image cannot be fetched
cleanup: The build context and archive are removed from the scratch directory, and every image this module creates is removed by tag on the way out. Ephemeral containers remove themselves; the health containers are removed when their Sandbox drops. Anything a killed run leaves behind carries this agent's label and is reaped at the start of the next one, images before containers.
limitations: Startup and health are measured against BusyBox rather than an application image, so they describe what the runtime costs and not what any particular application costs to boot. A real service adds its own start-up on top, and that part is a property of the service.

health.to_serving includes the runtime's port publication, which a container started without a published port does not pay. It is timed from the moment the container is asked for, because that is when an operator starts waiting.

The build is FROM scratch and runs with --network none, so no registry or package mirror is involved. That is deliberate: a build starting FROM a real base image would mostly measure a registry, which network.transfer measures directly and under a bounded ceiling.
This is the one module that writes to a host filesystem it cannot put on a tmpfs. The storage driver is configured daemon-wide and is not this program's to change - changing it would be T-CONFIG.
The layer cache is warmed by this module's own first build, so the cached figure is a best case. A CI cache that has to be restored from elsewhere pays a transfer this does not measure.

Every figure here measures the container daemon as much as the machine. The storage driver decides what a layer commit costs, and overlay2 on ext4 against the same silicon with a copy-on-write-whole-file driver differ by more than any two CPUs in this market do. The runtime is recorded in comparability so the comparison layer can refuse on evidence.

scoring.note: The builds carry the most weight because they are the longest thing in a deploy and the part an engineer waits through. cache.speedup carries the least despite being the most quotable: a ratio is not a speed, and a machine with a slow uncached build earns a large one for having had further to fall. Reference anchors are declared targets, not measurements, and are the least transferable in the model because they describe a storage driver as much as a machine. See docs/SCORING-SYSTEM.md.
